174.dq: Stress is not phonemic in this language. It occurs on the penultimate syllable of multisyllabic roots. Stress occurs consistently on the penultimate syllable of prefixed and infixed forms. In prefixed monosyllabic roots stress does not occur on the root, rather it occurs on the penultimate syllable of the prefixed form.
174.dloc: StressTyp2 entry for Kisar (Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015; entry), which digests Christensen & Christensen 1992: sec. 1.1 'Stress on root words' p. 34 (first two sentences) and the passage on prefixed and infixed forms p. 35 (last two sentences), joined without an elision mark
174.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (roots, prefixed, infixed and disyllabic-suffixed forms alike; unaffixed monosyllabic roots are stressed). Monosyllabic suffixes (e.g. possessive -e, -ne, plural -he) and the optional echo-vowel release of final consonants do not shift stress, so such forms are stressed on the antepenult (ˈraine, aˈnulue, ˈohorne, tataˈnenihe, ˈkaʔuku); a few frozen contractions (ˈnamene, haˈromene) and words in final /ia/ (enˈpenia) are lexical exceptions.
174.srule: Secondary stress on the second syllable to the left of the primary stress (ˌnam-kuˈkuru 'he is sleeping'); on alternating syllables leftward in longer words (editors' summary p.4; left-headed binary feet built from the right edge).

morph.elicq: Christensen & Christensen 1992:34-37 present stress only as impressionistic transcriptions of single words and short affixed/encliticised forms — ['ho.ro] 'cough', ['ra.in] 'dress', [ma'we.ke] 'girl', [na-'ʔa.han] 'he is angry', [na-'la.u] 'he laughs', ["nam-ku'ku.ru] 'he is sleeping', ['ka.ʔuk] ~ ['ka.ʔu.ku] 'afraid', [tata'nenihe] 'these children'. No stress-specific elicitation procedure, frame, connected-speech or instrumental evidence appears in the accessible text; the only provenance statement is general (p.34 fn.3): "Examples for this paper are taken from a beginning lexicon of 1,000+ words, a number of texts and conversations, and our field data ..." — procedure otherwise unstated.
morph.stmt: Kisar inflects verbs by prefix only — "it can be argued that every verb has an obligatory person-number prefix" showing subject agreement (Blood 1992:7; 'u-/m-/k-/n-/r-), which on consonant-initial verbs surfaces on the end of the preceding word or is lost — and reduplication is likewise prefixal (he-ha 'DUP-thing', ro-ropo), while everything else attested is post-posed or non-affixal: TAM enclitic -edi/-ale and particle me'e, inalienable possessor suffix -ne/-e/-'u, demonstrative (DEF) and plural enclitics -eni/-onne/-he on nouns, a nominalizing infix -nV-, and free particles for negation (preverbal ka), polar questions (clause-final ka) and modality (bisa, musti); Christensen &…

175.dq: The phonological word is a rhythm unit having one major stress placement, the physical manifestation of stress being relatively greater intensity often accompanied by relatively higher pitch. In general the boundaries of phonological and grammatical words coincide.
175.dloc: Davies 1981 [1989] Kobon (Rosetta scan), §3.2 'Phonotactics', p. 219; Davies 1980:58 "In phonological words of more than one syllable stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable" via Rasin 2017:26 (carried quote); StressTyp2 entry (Davies:58) + words ˈɱajə aˈrab aˈlafe danˈabel
175.heavy: the syllable whose vowel is stronger on Davies' hierarchy a/au/ai > o/e/u/i > ə/ɨ (relative vowel strength), within the last two syllables
175.srule: Not mentioned in Davies 1980 (§3.2.3.1 p. 22, §3.6.1-3.6.1.2 pp. 57-58 read): the phonological word is 'a rhythm unit having one major stress placement'; no secondary or rhythmic stresses are described, and every transcription (words up to five syllables) carries a single stress mark. Davies 1981:219 repeats the one-major-stress wording; Kenstowicz 1997 and Rasin 2018 do not discuss secondary stress.
175.quote: Although the rules for the placement of stress cannot be stated comprehensively at this stage, it appears that stress is not phonemic. In phonological words of more than one syllable stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable. [ˈbado] /bado/ 'men married to sisters', [aˈḷaβʌ] /aḷafə/ 'tree sp.', [ˈmandzʌ] /majə/ 'big', [dauˈambʌl] /dauabəl/ 'they are bringing', [dauaŋgəˈnambʌl] /dauagnabəl/ 'they will not bring', [dauˈaŋgənampʰ] /dauagnab/ 'he will not bring'. tn.quote: 3.6. A FEW COMMENTS ON THE HIGHER LEVELS The following remarks are very tentative. … 3.6.1. The Phonological Word The phonological word is composed of one to five syllables. It is a rhythm unit having one major stress placement, a composite of higher pitch and intensity. … it appears that stress is not phonemic. … 3.6.3. The Phonological Sentence The phonological sentence … is the unit of intonation placement in the phonological hierarchy. It is bounded by pause, and is characterised by an undulating intonation contour and a down-glide on the final syllable.

tn.note: No tone is described: pitch figures only as a component of the single, non-phonemic word stress (normally penultimate) and as sentence intonation with a final down-glide.

175.cfw: Davies 1980 says stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, but Davies 1981 says vowel strength conditions its position, and the reanalyses of his data split: Kenstowicz 1997 argues for sonority-driven stress within the last two syllables while Rasin 2018 finds only a near-tie between that and a penultimate rule with weight exceptions, so Shih and de Lacy 2019 list Kobon among the languages whose stress placement is disputed.

176.quote: 2.9 Word Stress The primary stress is on syllable 1 . There is very little stress on syllable 2. A secondary stress is often placed on syllable 3 of a word of four or more syllables. Syllables having a long vowel are stressed more than the equivalent ones containing a short vowel. The vowel quality is clearest in syllable 1 and usually least in syllable 2 where there is a frequent reduction of the vowel to [<?].

morph.rootq: §2.9 Word Stress (p.25): 'The primary stress is on syllable 1. There is very little stress on syllable 2. A secondary stress is often placed on syllable 3 of a word of four or more syllables. Syllables having a long vowel are stressed more than the equivalent ones containing a short vowel.' (Positions are counted in the word; no reference to root, stem or affixes. Cf. vowel allophony §2.3: '(i) In primary stressed syllable (syllable 1) ...'; '(vi) In syllable 3 of words of four or more syllables, with slight secondary stress, the allophones are as in syllable 1'.)
morph.elicq: §2.9 gives no statement of how stress was observed. The immediately preceding section §2.8.1 'Passage of Speech Analysed' says '... a passage of 100 words of continuous speech was analysed' (used for phoneme frequencies and syllables-per-word counts, text and translation on p.24-25), and ch.1 reports field recordings ('On my first field trip in April-May, 1966, I recorded at Davenport Reserve, Port Augusta and at Koonibba Mission, near Ceduna, a number of informants ...'); a footnote elsewhere notes 'this was repeated in isolation as /yabaridji/'. None of these is tied to the stress statement.
morph.stmt: Platt gives no one-line typological summary, but every bound morpheme he describes follows the stem: pronouns are 'Stem + Affixes' (ŋaju- + -lu/-nja/-la/-gu, §3.3.1), noun cases and the relators 'to/from/with/without' are suffixes (§3.4 table, §3.4.6), verb tense, mode, aspect and Negative 2 are endings on the verb stem (§3.1.7-3.1.17; the aspect affix is 'an affix preceding the Non-Past or Past Tense affix', i.e. still post-stem), and the verb-forming -bu-/-binj, -maninj, -(dj)arinj and participial -njdjala/-ra are suffixal (§3.1.12-13, §3.2); no prefix of any kind is described for Gugada…

ev.text: p. 40, §2.5 Stress, in full: "It is not predictable whether stress occurs on the penultimate or the ultimate syllable of monomorphemic words. Penultimate stress, however, is most common in Kola. It should be noted that stress falls only on the root and never on affixes or clitics. In addition, stress does not occur beyond the penult of the root. Examples of contrastive stress are shown below: /'ɸanen/ 'a bird of paradise' — /ɸa'nis/ 'bat' /'bobah/ 'fear' — /bo'bo/ 'baby' /'aka/ 'to, for' — /a'ka/ 'he eats' (from /a/ 'he' + /'ka/ 'eat') /'talah/ 'sit' — /ta'lah/ 'we sail' (from /ta/ 'we' + /'lah/ 'sail')" "Stress shifts when compounds and contractions undergo resyllabification. If the second…

p. 43 defines the phonological word as a stress group with one primary stress; §2.5 speaks of "primary word stress". The root-only restriction ("stress falls only on the root and never on affixes or clitics") is morphology-sensitivity inside the word, not phrasal prominence. §2.5 conditions nothing on syllable makeup; and the lexicon shows the contrast is weight-blind in both directions — the same CVC.CVC shape takes final stress in /kaw'law/, /dah'koh/ and penult in /'dewar/-type words; CV.CV takes both /'sofi/ and /bo'bo/.

morph.elicq: Takata & Takata 1992 p.31: 'The present study is based on data gathered over a period of three years in the two villages of Kolamar (Wahkolamah) and Marlasi (Medan) on the east coast of Kola island.' No statement of whether stress was judged from isolated words, frames, or texts; the stress examples are cited as isolated (mostly monomorphemic) words and short prefixed forms.
morph.stmt: Kola is mixed but verb-prefixing at its core: 'Verbs are obligatorily prefixed with subject agreement markers' (§2.6.1 p.54), the intransitivizer h- stands 'between the subject prefix and the verb root' (§2.6.2), the nominalizer yeh- is 'prefixed to a verb root' (§2.6.4), and partial reduplication is pre-root (al-palaw, as-bosil) or infixing; suffixes are the person markers — inalienable possessive suffixes on nouns (Table 1), object suffixes on transitive verbs and prepositions (Table 10), adjective person markers (Table 8) — and the animate numeral suffix -i.

181.prule: Primary accent on the first syllable of the stem, not of the word: prefixes are not counted, so prefixed disyllables (luvè, evè) are accented on their final syllable.
181.srule: Secondary, weaker accent on the penult when more than two syllables follow the stem-initial syllable (stems of four or more syllables; none in three-syllable stems); in verbs with two or more prefix syllables the first prefix syllable also takes a slight accent.
181.quote: ACCENT. The accent in Kongo falls upon the first syllable* of the stem. When more than two syllables follow the first syllable of the stem, a secondary and weaker accent falls upon the penult. It is upon the first syllable of the stem that the accent falls, not upon the first syllable of the word; prefixes, therefore, do not affect the question. If a verb possesses prefixes to the extent of two or more syllables, the first of such prefix-syllables receives also a slight accent.

morph.rootq: Bentley 1887:701 (ACCENT): "The accent in Kongo falls upon the first syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables follow the first syllable of the stem, a secondary and weaker accent falls upon the penult. It is upon the first syllable of the stem that the accent falls, not upon the first syllable of the word; prefixes, therefore, do not affect the question. If a verb possesses prefixes to the extent of two or more syllables, the first of such prefix-syllables receives also a slight accent." (p.702 adds: "The perfect of the applied form of the verb ... requires strong accentuation on the penult.")
morph.elicq: No method statement. The evidence given is lists of isolated words ("Examples. meso, lunza, lauka, nua, zengona, tantika, katuka ... sumbididilanga", p.701; "The following are instances of the position of the accent in words of two and more syllables bearing a prefix", p.701-702) plus impressionistic phrase-level observations: "When a monosyllable follows another word without any pause between them, the monosyllable draws the accent of the preceding word upon its final syllable ... Tunga e nzo: Build a house; [pronounced] tunganzo" (p.702-703).

II. The second kind of inflexion is by prefix. tn.quote: The pitch is of very great importance in the Kongo language, as every syllable has a special i)itch relatively to the other syllables, and if a syllable (especially the root-syllable in primitive words is pronounced in a wrong i)itch, it generally changes the word into an entirely different word. … although the ground-pitch may differ veiy much, there is actually in primitive words only three gradations of the ropt-pitch: high, semi-high, and semi-low in the verbs; and high, acute, and semi-low in the nouns.

tn.note: Lexical pitch on every syllable, root pitch in three grades (high, semi-high, semi-low) with falling, level or rising word melody; separate root stress and penult rhythmic stress, influenced by pitch.

182.dq: Stress is predictable for most of the words in Korafe. Non-verbs and verb stems manifest word stress on: (1) the initial syllable of words with two syllables (2) the second syllable of words with more than two syllables, or (3) the first (C)VV(V) syllable (when this pattern occurs). In inflected verb forms, stress falls on the initial vowel of vowel-initial suffixes ...
182.dloc: Farr 1996:22, sec. 1.5 (ANU PhD thesis; = Farr 1999 PL C-148:14)
182.heavy: (C)VV(V) syllables: phonemic vowel length (written VV) and heterogeneous vowel sequences ('bimoric complex nuclei'), incl. V1V2V2 triple nuclei; the language has no closed syllables (inventory V, CV, VV, CVV, VVV, CVVV), so codas play no role.
182.dflt: initial syllable in two-syllable words; second (peninitial) syllable in words of three or more syllables
182.prule: Non-verbs and verb stems: (1) initial syllable in disyllables; (2) second syllable in words of more than two syllables; (3) overriding both, the first (C)VV(V) syllable when one occurs. Residue of lexically stressed words marked with acute accent (e.g. biká; OPD minimal pairs 'oka/o'ka, 'ofofo/o'fofo, 'joka/jo'ka).
182.srule: Not mentioned in Farr 1996 (sec. 1.5 pp. 21-22 = Farr 1999 PL C-148 pp. 12-14; ch. 3 fn. 5 p. 95; sec. 4.7.1 pp. 195-197) or in the SIL OPD Korafe p. 4: the source gives only the primary ('inherently stressed syllable') rule and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.

[p.22] Stress is predictable for most …
182.loc: Farr 1996 thesis pp. 21-22, section 1.5 Phonology, incl. fn. 20-21; OPD p. 4 'Suprasegmentals'
182.idn: Korafe (the 'main dialect' of Korafe, as opposed to Mokorua, 'also called Yegha'); data primarily from Baga village (a named variety of the language); data: villages on the headlands around Cape Nelson (Tufi), Oro Province, PNG; data primarily collected in the village of Baga, SIL research from 1972…
182.exq_: Stress is predictable for most of the words in Korafe. ... Where stress is not predictable, an acute accent (´) is written over the most sonorous vowel in the stressed syllable. [p.21] biká [biᵊ.'kʰa] 'sister-in-law' receiving stress on its second syllable [OPD p.4] 'oka 'fish' o'ka 'lime, limepot'
182.tone: No tone in Farr 1996: fn. 20 notes that Farr and Farr (1974:26) had interpreted the phonemic vowel length as word tone ('a slight down glide often does accompany the lengthened vowel'); a heavy (stressed) syllable 'may also manifest increased amplitude and a higher pitch'.

182.cfw: Farr's 1996 reference grammar, backed by the acute marks on the 6,949 headwords of Farr and Farr's 2008 dictionary, describes weight-sensitive stress (the first long-vowel syllable, otherwise the first syllable of two-syllable words and the second syllable of longer words), while the fixed initial stress reported by StressTyp2 and Gordon 2002 goes back to Farr and Farr's 1974 preliminary phonology, which Farr 1996 explicitly revises, so a single fieldwork lineage gives a clear winner with no independent confirmation.

morph.elicq: Word stress, impressionistic, from word lists: 'the difference in amplitude and tone between, say the two syllables of the word [gote] "stream" is minimal. In word lists the informants sometimes strike up a "slight fall" tone pattern with roughly equal amplitude, or sometimes a "slight rise" pattern accompanied by a slight drop in amplitude' (§3.3.2.2.1 p.430); 'The article a which precedes almost every word of a word list has a considerably lower amplitude and lower tone than the following noun' (§3.3.2.2.2 p.430). morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: 'The only way to derive (a word of) one morphological category from another in Koromfe, apart from compound nouns, is by the addition of a suffix' (§2.2 p.317); 'Koromfe has only one type of noun inflection, which is the system of noun classes. A noun class suffix expresses number and in addition (sometimes) other semantic characteristics of the noun, like humanness, diminutive, mass/liquid' (§2.1.1 p.149); the verb has 'only four inflectional morphological categories' - bare stem, PAST suffix -ɛ, DURATIVE suffix -d, PROGRESSIVE -aa added to the durative (§2.1.3 p.266). Person, negation, definiteness and possession are carried by separate (clitic or free) words…

qtr.text: In the overwhelming majority of cases the stress in disyllabic words falls on the first syllable ... A tendency has been noted to place the stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. ... In polysyllabic words (of more than four syllables) stressed and unstressed syllables alternate fairly evenly ... The division of stress into primary and secondary has so far been made for Koryak only very provisionally.

dqtr.text: Determining by ear the place of stress in a Koryak word is often quite difficult. [...] word stress [...] A description of intonation lies outside the scope of a description of the phonology of the word.

184.dq: Определить на слух место ударения в корякском слове часто бывает весьма затруднительно. [...] словесное ударение [...] Описание интонации выходит за рамки описания фонологии слова.

184.srule: Rhythmic beats, unranked: in words of three or more syllables 'stress falls on every second syllable, starting from the second syllable, excluding the final syllable' (Kurebito 2004:142, all beats marked alike); Zhukova 1972:41: in words of more than four syllables stressed and unstressed syllables alternate 'относительно равномерно' (010100, 10100, 010100), main vs secondary distinguished only 'весьма условно'.
184.quote: В подавляющем большинстве случаев ударение в двусложных словах падает на первый слог ... Отмечена тенденция — помещать ударение на предпоследний слог слова. ... В многосложных (более четырех слогов) словах относительно равномерно чередуются ударные и безударные слоги ... Разграничение ударения на главное и второстепенное проведено для корякского языка пока весьма условно.

secx.sec_quote_tr: In polysyllabic words (more than four syllables) stressed and unstressed syllables alternate relatively evenly, e.g. məč|čáj|go|čáw'|ŋə|la 'we studied', čáw'|čə|w'áč|h'e|ŋaŋ 'in Koryak', ga|wé|tan'|ŋwó|la|ta 'work a while!'. The demarcation of stress into main and secondary has so far been drawn for Koryak only very tentatively.
secx.primary_revised_quote: In two-syllable words, the accent generally falls on the first syllable. ... In words with more than two syllables, stress falls on every second syllable, starting from the second syllable, excluding the final syllable. [tə.qóː.dʒa.nóː.ma.káː.vək] 'I herded the reindeer.' ... However, if the vowel of the second syllable is schwa, the stress falls regressively on the first syllable.

185.prule: Every word is accented (stressed) on its first syllable, a monosyllable on its only syllable; all other syllables of the word are unaccented. Within a phrase the accent of the first word is the primary stress accent and that of each succeeding word a secondary stress accent.

Its Kota entry in the language list points at Emeneau for the language: '10. Kota. Pop. 1,400. Mainly craftsmen among the Nilgiri tribes. Emeneau (1944–6).'. Sec. 2.4.1 'Stress and intonation' (pp. No Kota-specific stress sentence is on record from this work. Not instrumental; no material measured.

186.srule: Non-primary stress is weight-conditioned, not quantity-insensitive: 'Within a word stress occurs with long syllables... Weak stress occurs with short syllables' (Tyler 1969:32; his long-syllable templates read (C)V̄, CV̄C, CVC, CVNC with macrons restored -- the scan prints '(C)V, CVC, CVC CVNG'; StressTyp2/Hayes 1980 render it as secondary stress on closed syllables and syllables with a long vowel, e.g. ˈənˌdooru 'everyone'). These stresses follow weight, so they are not written into the count grid. Tyler also notes strong stress on the final syllable of a sequence before a terminal juncture under a falling intonation contour (p. 33).

morph.stmt: Mosel 1984:4-5 characterises Tolai as near-isolating in its grammatical relations — "activity and inactivity are not distinguished morphologically, but instead by word order... Non-derived transitive verbs are reduplicated when used intransitively..., whereas simple intransitive verbs, when they are used transitively, must be transformed into transitive verbs by so-called 'transitive suffixes'... Furthermore, Tolai lacks bound morphemes indicating case and the category of passive voice"; subject, tense/aspect/mood, negation, articles and plural are preposed particles (NEG SM TA ADV V... E, p.95), while the bound morphology is split: derivational prefixes and left-edge processes…

morph.rootq: Murkelinskij 1967:490, sec.4: «Ударение в лакском языке слабое, непостоянное и в известной степени связано с долготой гласного. Но в ряде морфологических форм оно фиксировано на закрытом слоге: зу́нтту 'гора', хъу́нтIа 'яма', буру́ккин 'забота', и словообразовательных суффиксах: къалайчи́ 'лудильщик', чичáву 'писание', гъанмá 'тот, который близок'.» [Stress in Lak is weak, not fixed, and to a certain extent tied to vowel length. But in a number of morphological forms it is fixed on the closed syllable ... and on word-forming suffixes: q'alajči 'tinsmith', čičawu 'writing', hanma 'the one who is near'.] Secondary (Borise, carrying Murkelinskij 1971:55): 'Exceptionally, certain suffixes…
morph.elicq: Murkelinskij 1967:490 gives only isolated citation forms with an accent mark (зу́нтту 'гора', хъу́нтIа 'яма', буру́ккин 'забота', къалайчи́ 'лудильщик', чичáву 'писание', гъанмá) and states no elicitation method. Borise (p.7): 'because stress in Lak is acoustically weak (Khajdakov 1999: 91), it has been hypothesized that Lak relies on phrasal prominence only (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 334). However, Zhirkov (1955: 15) notes that Lak speakers have consistent intuitions about its placement.' - i.e. impressionistic/intuition-based, no frames or instrumental data reported.
morph.stmt: Schulze 2007 sec.2.7.1 characterises the Lak verb as 'Prefixing (class and (older) preverbs) - suffixing (TAM) - clitisizing (fPAM [floating person-agreement enclitics])', and the noun as base form + stem augment + case/plural suffixes (sec.2.2: 'OBL = BF + SA:SG + CASE; PL = BF + PL'): Lak is predominantly suffixing/encliticising, the only pre-root bound material being the gender-class agreement markers b-/d-/Ø- (also infixed -w-/-r- inside discontinuous stems) and the negators q:a-/ma- (which may also be endoclitic); in the 80-word running-text sample 22 prefix morphs (all class markers or q:a-) stand against 77 suffix/enclitic morphs.

morph.rootq: None of the open sources used contains a statement about word stress or accent in Juǀ'hoan; they describe it as a tone language whose lexical words fit bimoraic root templates: 'Juǀ'hoan has rigid phonotactic templates for lexical and grammatical words typical of "Khoisan" languages. Lexical words are essentially bimoraic and adhere to three basic patterns: CVCV, CVV, and CVN ... Conceivably, -mà and -mhí have been reduced to a monomoraic CV template reserved for functional words' (Pratchett 2021: 287). The stress coding for this language rests on Snyman 1970 via Gordon 2002, which was not accessible.
morph.elicq: No stress description in the sources used. (For the record, the only openly available prosodic remark found is for a SISTER lect, Doke 1925 on the Neitsas/Nurugas ʗhũ: = Central Ju, glottocode cent2300, not juho1239: 'Stress, however, is not so important a subject. Since, to a great extent, the structure of the language is monosyllabic, tone rather than stress composes the sentence rhythm. However, in certain words where there are more syllables than one, it is found that a certain stress occurs on the syllable containing a long vowel' (Bantu Studies 2: 'Length and Stress'); evidence base there = five weeks of vocabulary elicitation with named informants, i.e. isolated words.)
morph.stmt: 'Ju is a highly isolating language with two main open word classes, namely nouns and verbs... tn.quote: Each type of root can have either one or two tones, but roots with interrupted vowels have an affinity towards being bitonal. There are four tone levels, but only six of the predicted tonal patterns are attested on verb roots. Verbs bear all four level tones, plus two of the three possible combinations of rising tones. The third possible rising tone, H SH, occurs only very rarely on nouns. This is expected, since SH tones are in general very rare. ... I argue that this disparity arises because the tone bearing unit being is the mora.
tn.cite: Miller-Ockhuizen, Amanda. 1999 [2000]. Reduplication in Ju|’hoansi: Tone Determines Weight. In M. Hirotani (ed.), Proceedings of NELS 29. Amherst: GLSA / University of Massachusetts Occasional Papers in Linguistics (author-posted copy).
tn.locator: p.2, §2.0 'Overview of Ju|’hoansi Prosody' (before ex.2); last sentence p.7, §5.0
tn.note: Four level tones (SL, L, H, SH), at most one per mora; roots monotonal or bitonal (rising = two levels; HL only on loans); downstep in reduplication; on stress only 'little evidence for feet' (p.14).

189.cfw: The initial-stress coding rests only on the StressTyp2 and Gordon 2002 survey entries, which take it second-hand from Snyman 1970 (not read), while Downing 2004 reports that Ju|'hoan and the other Khoisan languages are described as tone languages with no discussion of stress in the literature, so the record is a guess until a first-hand description is read.

Most grammatical elements added to nouns (-ek, -ê, -a) are enclitic and thus unstressed (miróv > miróvek, gúnd > gúndê, odé > odéya), with the exception of the plural suffixes -ên and -an, which are stressed (kúrd > kurdê´n, kurdán). The hierarchy of stress in verbs is as follows: (1) The negative prefixes na- and ne- ... (2) Preverbs like ve-, hil-, da-, and wer- ... (3) The modal prefixes di- and bi- ... (4) When there are no prefixes on finite verbal forms, the final syllable of the verb stem is stressed, as in axíftine 'they have spoken.' (5) The infinitive is stressed on the final syllable."…
morph.elicq: No statement of evidence type; the stress section (p.4) simply asserts "Stress. All nouns and adjectives are lightly stressed on the final syllable..." with broad IPA transcriptions of citation forms (e.g. náçim [»nAtSˆm] 'I don't go', axiftín [AxIf»tIn] 'to speak'); it is a pedagogical reference grammar of the written standard with no described fieldwork, frames, or measurements.
morph.stmt: Thackston gives no single typological sentence, but his description amounts to: nominal morphology is entirely post-root (oblique -ê/-an, construct -ê/-a/-ên, plural -an/-ên, "Most grammatical elements added to nouns (-ek, -ê, -a) are enclitic and thus unstressed", p.4), while the finite verb is mixed: stressed pre-root negation ná-/né-, aspect dí-, subjunctive bí- and preverbs (ve-, hil-, da-, wer-, ra-, der-) combine with unstressed person-number suffixes and suffixal perfect/conditional endings ("the stressed progressive/habitual modal marker dí is prefixed to the present stem, and the following suffixed personal endings are added to the stem", §14 p.33); derivation…

191.exc_quote: The exceptions to Penultimate Stress Assignment are, for the most part, words from French having word-final stress. These words include a very few borrowed lexical items and most of the Christian names in Kutenai. There are also a very few words of native origin which have word-final stress. There is the word /taxtá·/ 'later', and there is a phrase reported by Garvin (1948a, p. 38) which has phrase-final stress, and is made of native material. It is /hu‿sɬ‿táɬ/ 'I am not able', a verbal phrase missing the verbal stem. (Morgan 1991: 112, fn. 3)

191.sec_rule: Rhythmical Stress Assignment (Morgan: 'some evidence for'): still weaker stresses on every second syllable counting back from the penultimate (main-stressed) syllable to the beginning of the phrase; a rhythmical stress adjacent to a word-stressed syllable is not realized, and rhythmical stress differs little phonetically from no stress (p. 120). Within a phrase, non-final words keep a weaker penultimate word stress unless it is adjacent to the phrasal stress. Garvin 1948:38 (via StressTyp2) described the same alternation as 'automatic secondary stress on every second syllable preceding the primarily stressed syllable'.
191.sec_quote: There is also some evidence for a rule of Rhythmical Stress Assignment which assigns still weaker instances of stress to every second syllable of a phrase, starting with the penultimate syllable of the phrase, counting back every other syllable to the beginning of the phrase.

192.sec_rule: Stated, placed by morphology (Keesing 1985:9-13): in polymorphemic (affixed or reduplicated) forms each (C)VCV or CVV sequence takes a full or partial stress on its penultimate vowel; the major stress is the one on the penultimate vowel of the final segment, earlier ones are minor (laalama; kolo-te'e-ni-a, garugaru-mi-a with stresses on vowels 1-3-5; but oriori-si-a, taatake-ni-a, siisina-fi-a with the medial base unstressed, vowels 1 and 5 only). Analyzable trisyllables: penultimate stress with secondary stress on the first syllable (wa-siu, ma-bota); unanalyzable trisyllabic bases: roughly equal stress on the first two vowels (adalo).
192.sec_quote: p. 13: "Within each sequence (C)VCV or CVV, a full or partial stress is given to the penultimate vowel. This pattern is preserved in reduplication (´ is minor or single stress, ˝ is major stress in a form with two or more stressed syllables)"; p. 10: "A trisyllabic form that is analyzable ... is pronounced with stress on the penultimate vowel, with secondary stress on the first syllable."

morph.elicq: The stress section (§2.3.2 p.89) gives no evidential basis: "It most often occurs on the penultimate syllable, but there are exceptions. As with tone, more work needs to be done in this area." The only statement about data in general is §1.3.1 p.85: "We began working with informants John Kosu and Conelly Aima at the university and also conducted field work at Labubutu ... I worked with Keith Kamake from Labubutu" — nothing specific to how stress was observed (§2.3.1 p.89 does show two sentence pitch contours for tone, not stress).
morph.stmt: Labu inflection is exclusively prefixal and confined to the verb — "Verbs are the class of words which consist of a verbal prefix... plus a verb stem" (§4.1 p.97), summarised as "Vb -> STM (-CTF) -stem (INC)" (§4.1.8 p.102) — while nouns are uninflected ("no productive possessive suffixes" §3.5.2 p.95; "There is no productive way of forming nouns from verbs", only a vestigial nominaliser -ya, §3.1.2 p.92), and aspect, modality particles, negation, possession, demonstratives and case-like relations are all free words (postverbal sô/papa, preverbal ŋgwa/wa/mba, clause-final ki, prepositions and serial verbs).

tn.quote: Stress accent plays an important role in Dakota. We may distinguish between accented words and unaccented parts of speech, enclitics and proclitics … Syllables bearing the main accent have a high pitch. In rapid speech discrimination between accented and unaccented syllables or those having a secondary accent may be recognized more readdy by pitch than by stress. Miss Deloria decides in all doubtful cases the question whether the syllables are accented or not, by pitch. The accent is not firmly attached to any particular syllable, but has a definite relation to the position of the syllable.
tn.cite: Boas, Franz & Ella Deloria. 1941. Dakota Grammar. Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. XXIII, Second Memoir. Washington: United States Government Printing Office.
tn.note: No lexical tone is described: a stress accent, mostly on the second syllable, whose accented syllable carries high pitch; in rapid speech pitch is the clearer cue to the accent. A second reading (Carter 1974): No distinctive tone or length; pitch (with loudness) marks stress; pitch contour of a trisyllable with 2nd-syllable stress given as mid-high-low (p. 270). Primary stress on 2nd underlying stem vowel.

194.cfw: Boas & Deloria 1941, Van Valin 1977, Rood & Taylor 1996 and Mirzayan 2010 all put Lakota main stress on the second syllable by rule, and differ from the catalog only in insisting that the rule has a residue of lexical exceptions (šúŋka 'dog', thípi 'house', líla 'very', rare tuktená), so second-syllable stress is secure but not exceptionless.

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Solorese: In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable.". The source gives: Penultimate stress; if the penult (of a disyllable, per Kroon) contains schwa, stress falls on the final syllable; monosyllables stressed with a lengthened vowel. — StressTyp2 codes plain penult (STC P / 2R, 'penultimate in words of all sizes'), which matches the default but drops the schwa-penult -> final clause that both its own Arndt passage and its ST1 note (': full vowels') record; the source is weight-sensitive on vowel quality, not quantity-insensitive.

ev.text: 3.4 Stress patterns. SL has a fixed stress pattern. It is commonly assigned to a penultimate syllable, a characteristic which is typical of Austronesian languages – see e.g. Blust (2013: 251), Nishiyama and Kellen (2007: 11). However, when the penultimate syllable in a disyllabic word contains a schwa, such as gedã [gə.`dã] ‘drum’ and lenga [lə.`ŋa] ‘fall’, stress falls on the ultimate syllable. For a monosyllabic word, stress falls on the full phonological word, in which the vowel tends to be phonologically longer. 195.dq: Solor has words consisting of from one to five syllables. The word accent in words without suffixes usually falls on the penultimate syllable. If this syllable contains a schwa it sometimes falls on the stem-final syllable. When suffixes are added to a stem the accent in by far most cases remains on the originally accented syllable. 195.heavy: A penult whose nucleus is schwa /ə/ fails to hold stress (stress goes to the final); syllables with full (non-schwa) vowels hold penult stress. No role stated for codas or vowel length (length is allophonic, longer under stress / in monosyllables).

morph.rootq: Mwape 2012 gives no stress description (only tone and vowel length: 'Lamba has two suprasegmental features: viz length and tone', p.25). The stress statement behind our coding is Doke 1938:33, as block-quoted in Hyman 2013: 'The stress in Lamba is normally on the penultimate syllable of each word, and in this way is to a great extent the determining factor in word-division.… Unlike Zulu the penultimate stress is not of necessity accompanied by length. Penultimate length is merely incidental in Lamba.' — the domain named is the word, not the root/stem.
morph.elicq: Only the Doke 1938:33 block quote is available ('The stress in Lamba is normally on the penultimate syllable of each word …'); it says nothing about how stress was observed, and Doke 1938 itself could not be consulted. (Mwape 2012's own tonal data, not stress, came from questionnaire sentences translated by informants: 'All the sentences were in English and the informants were asked to translate them into Lamba. The interviews were tape-recorded and later transcribed phonetically. In the absence of equipment for determining tone, the researcher relied on his ears', p.7.)
morph.stmt: 'The structure of the Lamba verb is similar to that of all other Bantu languages which … comprises a radical and several affixes which precede it or follow it' (Mwape 2012:37): pre-prefix (negative ta-), subject prefix, tense/aspect sign and object 'infix' precede the radical, while extensions, the final vowel/ending and the post-ending -po follow it (Fig. 6, p.38: ta-Ba-lúku-mu-lim-in-a-po 'they are not cultivating for him'); nouns are marked only by prefixes (augment + class prefix, incl. plural, diminutive ka-/tu- and locative pa-/ku-/mu-), so inflection is predominantly prefixing with a suffixal layer of TAM endings and derivational extensions. Token indices after adjudication…

Where the root is longer than one syllable — only possible in nouns — the first vowel receives stress.... Stressed vowels in Lango are somewhat louder and slightly longer than unstressed vowels. morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined appears in the accessible text (the one-page Sec. 3, p. 42, is known only through the StressTyp2/Hyman excerpts, which give the rule and an impressionistic phonetic remark: "Stressed vowels are somewhat louder and slightly longer than unstressed vowels. morph.stmt: Lango is a lightly agglutinating, mixed prefixing-suffixing language (WALS 26A-lan 'equal prefixing and suffixing') whose verb morphology is being levelled: the finite verb is [subject prefix a-/i-/o- (+ narrative tɛ-)] + ROOT + [stem vowel / benefactive -i / middle-reflexive -ɛrɛ / object suffix], with aspect and mood carried by tone and stem gemination, tense by preverbal auxiliaries and negation by a preverbal particle pé; nouns take only suffixes (possessor -ná/-ní/-ɛ́/-wa/-gí, determiners -nì/-cà, indefinite -mórò, plural -e/-i/-ni on a minority of nouns) and no case, relations being carried by free prepositions (ì, mê, bòt, kèdè). 199.exc_quote: Noonan 1992:42 (StressTyp2 passage 1260): 'Particles, prepositions with noun objects, and certain prepositions following verbs are not stressed. Instead, they cliticize to the adjacent stressed form. In reduplicated words, stress is placed on the last unreduplicated syllable.' StressTyp2 lect 641 exceptions note (source: Noonan): 'In a few words ending on /l/, stress is placed on the last syllable.' — example dàkˈtàl 'doctor'.

excx.count_based_why: stress placement is set by the morphology

199.sec_quote: Downing 2010:393: "Stress, realized as increased amplitude and length, is regularly assigned to the root- (stem?) initial vowel, as shown in (7a). Only borrowed words have stress on other root syllables. In compounds, the rightmost word of the compound receives primary stress, as shown in (7b). (7) Lango stress (Noonan 1992, pp. 42–43)". StressTyp2 lect 641: secondary = 'No information'.
